newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president now under pressure from Moscow.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president now under pressure from Moscow.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko, under pressure from Moscow to compromise with his opponents, is a master of populist rhetoric whose promises of a Soviet-style better future have struck a chord with less educated voters.
But his critics say he is an authoritarian would-be dictator who has plunged his small country into confrontation and economic decline.

"From November 25 we will put things straight and everyone will have to work," the defiant leader told supporters at a rally on Monday. "Whoever doesn't want this will have to find another motherland."

The next day, campaigning in the small town of Borisov, he won over a crowd of several thousand with emotionally charged references to World War Two and the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, both of which left more devastation in Belarus than anywhere else.

"You should not fear, there is no dictatorship, there is no fascism, and fascism will never return to our land," he told the crowd, which interrupted his 30-minute speech several times with rapturous applause and cries of "Hurrah! Hurrah!"
"We will live together. We will build this life together. I promise you that I will always be with you. Only you have the right to criticise, strike or beat up the president," he said.
The crowd, mostly elderly, were overwhelmed by the appearance of their lean, angular, moustachioed president who they call "batska" in Belarussian -- or father.
One pensioner explained why he would support Lukashenko. "He's a great man. He speaks for the people. He lives for the people. We really like him because he speaks so simply and so clearly."
The crisis in Belarus is being compared to the run-up to a bloody conflict in Russia in 1993, which President Boris Yeltsin ended by sending tanks against parliament.

But Lukashenko has some experience of his own of such stand-offs. Last year he ordered police to evict several liberal deputies who went on hunger strike to protest against his policies. They were beaten by police in the chamber.
Communists, liberals and nationalists have joined forces to oppose Lukashenko and his authoritarian style of rule.
But there is a lack of strong opposition leadership in this nation of 10 million sandwiched between Russia and Poland.

Lukashenko's parliamentary opponents compare him to World War Two dictators -- Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. Last year Lukashenko himself in an interview with a German newspaper praised Hitler for his strong rule in pre-war Germany.

Lukashenko, 42, was born in the village of Kopys in eastern Belarus. In Soviet days he was a "politruk" or political instructor in the Soviet Army, a low-level activist in the Komsomol youth organisation and then took over a state farm.
He began his rise to power as the head of parliament's anti-corruption commission, winning the presidency by a landslide in July 1994.

His sensational statements about high-level corruption brought him political glory and popularity among impoverished Belarussians, and his policy of forming a union with Russia struck a chord with a nation struggling to define itself.

As economic crisis has deepened, he has stepped up his pro-Russian rhetoric and pressed Russian leaders for a closer union. Last April he and Russian President Boris Yeltsin signed a pact forming a community, but politicians in Moscow are increasingly wary of Lukashenko.
"Lukashenko's personal ambitions...gave him a feeling of claustrophobia on Belarus's political stage. He dreams of playing on the Russian one," the Moscow daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta wrote this week.
Lukashenko regularly ignores the constitution and Belarussian law, and he has kept tight controls on the media.

There is no strong opposition party and no independent media in Belarus. Lukashenko banned independent trade unions, sacked newspaper editors and closed radio stations. He even threatened this week to expel two Russian television journalists.

He shows open nostalgia for the Soviet Union, and pushed through a decision at a referendum in May 1995 to replace new state symbols with Soviet-style ones. But he now favours Orthodox Christianity rather than Marxism-Leninism.

Last year, after his forces shot down an air balloon killing two American pilots taking part in an international race, Lukashenko appologised and then praised his military for "high level of readiness."
Belarus is the only European state outside former Yugoslavia which has yet to join the Council of Europe and has been permanently accused by human rights watchdogs of abuses.
